title: Multi-Agent AI Systems Must Work Like An Orchestra Without A Conductor
gist: In a closed-door DAC roundtable, EDA leaders from Cadence, Synopsys, Siemens EDA, Keysight EDA and ChipAgents describe multi-agent chip-design AI shifting from hierarchical 'armies' to flat, headless 'orchestras,' while warning that the 'march of nines' accuracy requirement, IP/copyright exposure of prompts, on-prem compute shortages, and token costs remain the binding constraints on full autonomy.

themes.theme: Multi-agent architecture: flat orchestras, not armies

insights.claim: Multi-agent AI systems in chip design have shifted within about a year from an anticipated rigid military-style hierarchy (generals, lieutenants, sub-agents) to a much flatter, dynamic, task-based assembly of skills with one orchestrator/commander coordinating specialized agents.
insights.speaker: Matt Graham
insights.so_what: Vendors building agent orchestration tooling should design for dynamic skill assembly rather than fixed pipelines; investors should expect EDA agent products to differentiate on orchestration flexibility, not just raw agent count.
insights.quote: We’re not bound, as armies are, by logistical and physical reality.
insights.locator: Graham: It is becoming much flatter than an army

insights.claim: Alexander Petr of Keysight EDA frames the ideal multi-agent structure as an orchestra with one conductor and instrument groups that can play individually or together, synchronously or asynchronously, all grounded by shared borders and guardrails.
insights.speaker: Alexander Petr
insights.so_what: This orchestra framing signals that EDA vendors see value in coordinated-but-decentralized agent design over single monolithic controller agents, a design pattern investors can look for in product roadmaps.
insights.quote: You’re better off comparing it to an orchestra. You have one conductor, and you have groups who play certain instruments.
insights.locator: Petr: You’re better off comparing it to an orchestra

insights.claim: Siemens EDA is building toward 'headless' agentic systems with no master agent, where deterministic physical/simulation engines themselves become agents that talk to other agents, and end customers interact with tools without knowing which underlying agent is doing the work.
insights.speaker: Sathish Balasubramanian
insights.so_what: Watch for Siemens EDA (and peers) to embed agent interfaces directly into simulation/physics engines rather than bolting on a separate chat layer -- a product architecture shift that could redefine EDA tool interfaces industry-wide.
insights.quote: There’s no concept of having a big master agent doing everything else. We call it a headless way of working, and it’s been quite popular on the software side. It’s coming here.
insights.locator: Balasubramanian: The term I see quite a bit is headless agents

insights.claim: Synopsys frames the shift as organizations needing a fluid (not rigid) orchestration layer that calls upon agent 'resources' dynamically depending on task complexity, with the system potentially becoming autonomous in the future once more abstraction layers are removed -- but that future state is not yet reached.
insights.speaker: Anand Thiruvengadam
insights.so_what: Full autonomy remains a stated future milestone rather than current reality per a Synopsys AI product leader -- useful calibration against more aggressive AI-autonomy marketing claims elsewhere in the industry.
insights.quote: At some point in the future, it might graduate to something where it’s maybe autonomous. That is about abstraction again... but we’re not there yet.
insights.locator: Thiruvengadam: What Matt said is very interesting

themes.theme: The accuracy ceiling: the 'march of nines' limits full autonomy

insights.claim: Matt Graham (Cadence) argues that expecting 100% agentic autonomy in chip design is unrealistic and not worthwhile, drawing a parallel to RTL synthesis: even though the vast majority of gates are now synthesized, a meaningful percentage of design still requires hand-synthesis or hand-layout, and agentic tools will likely follow the same pattern of high-but-incomplete automation.
insights.speaker: Matt Graham
insights.so_what: Investors should discount claims of near-total design automation from AI-in-EDA vendors; the realistic near/mid-term model is high-leverage augmentation with a persistent human/hand-coded tail, similar to synthesis adoption history.
insights.quote: Expecting 100% autonomy is setting too high a bar that I don’t know we can achieve. I don’t think it’s realistic or even worthwhile.
insights.locator: Graham: There are two sides to that

insights.claim: In chip design, being 99.99% accurate counts as failure because a single picosecond timing error creates a full design violation, making the reliability bar for agentic/AI tools in EDA fundamentally higher than in most software applications.
insights.speaker: Sathish Balasubramanian
insights.so_what: This sets a much higher bar for AI adoption in physical/electrical design flows than in general software agents -- a structural reason EDA AI adoption may lag consumer/enterprise software AI adoption despite similar model capability.
insights.quote: In chip design, being 99.99% accurate is a failure. All it takes is one picosecond and you have a whole violation.
insights.locator: Balasubramanian: That’s very important. In chip design

insights.claim: Keysight EDA's Alexander Petr contends that despite advances in agentic AI frameworks, mathematically based deterministic optimizers remain faster and more accurate than reinforcement-learning-based probabilistic approaches for physics-based EDA problems, because every AI model is a simplification layered with compounding error on top of still-incomplete physics understanding.
insights.speaker: Alexander Petr
insights.so_what: A contrarian signal from an EDA insider that RL/agentic approaches are not yet displacing classical deterministic solvers in core physics-heavy EDA tasks -- relevant for evaluating hype around 'AI replaces simulators' narratives.
insights.quote: It’s an error of an error of an error of an error... my mathematically based optimizer is still faster and more accurate. Why would I want to do that?
insights.locator: Petr: We keep forgetting that we still have not fully understood all the physics

insights.claim: Synopsys's Anand Thiruvengadam argues the 'march of nines' reliability problem is inherently worse in hardware than software because hardware failure costs are far higher, making the bar for AI to subsume core EDA tool functions correspondingly higher.
insights.speaker: Anand Thiruvengadam
insights.so_what: Cost-of-failure asymmetry between software and hardware is a durable moat protecting incumbent deterministic EDA tool vendors (Cadence, Synopsys, Siemens) from being fully displaced by generative AI agents.
insights.quote: In hardware, costs are so high that the march of nines becomes an even bigger problem.
insights.locator: Thiruvengadam: It’s important to understand that the march of nines is a problem in software

themes.theme: Context management, not agent count, is the real bottleneck

insights.claim: ChipAgents' Harrison Balistreri argues that throwing more agents at a problem does not improve outcomes if all agents share the same local context, because they will converge on similar hypotheses regardless of how many agents or how good the judging agent is; the real lever is managing local-vs-global context diversity across agents.
insights.speaker: Harrison Balistreri
insights.so_what: For investors evaluating agentic AI startups, agent-count or parallelism claims are a weak signal; the differentiator to diligence is whether a vendor has engineered genuine context diversity across agents.
insights.quote: It doesn’t matter how many agents you deploy or how good your judging agent is... it doesn’t matter how you deploy agents if they all have the same local context.
insights.locator: Balistreri: We have products where agents propose hypotheses

insights.claim: Balistreri states that agents become powerful only when they can deliver the full design flow rather than performing narrow 'point acceleration' on a single tool, requiring an encoded ontology that captures how context should be viewed and managed across the flow.
insights.speaker: Harrison Balistreri
insights.so_what: Point-solution AI tools bolted onto single EDA steps are likely to underperform full-flow agentic platforms -- a consolidation thesis favoring vendors that can span RTL-to-GDS rather than a single tool.
insights.quote: You can’t just do point acceleration around one tool. Agents become powerful when they can deliver the full flow.
insights.locator: Balistreri: I want to recap a bit

insights.claim: One of the biggest bottlenecks customers report in taping out chips is insufficient on-premises compute to run existing EDA tools -- a constraint that predates and compounds the added compute/token demands of agentic AI layered on top.
insights.speaker: Harrison Balistreri
insights.so_what: On-prem compute capacity is a real, near-term constraint on EDA AI adoption -- relevant to demand forecasts for compute infrastructure and cloud EDA offerings serving the semiconductor design industry.
insights.quote: One of the biggest bottlenecks in taping out their chips is that they don’t have enough on-premises compute to run existing EDA tools.
insights.locator: Balistreri: This might be an unpopular opinion in this room

themes.theme: IP ownership and copyright risk in AI-generated chip designs

insights.claim: Sathish Balasubramanian states that a designer's prompts to an AI agent effectively constitute their proprietary IP/IQ (the encoded methodology for solving a design problem, e.g. routing), and that any prompt sent outside an air-gapped environment to an LLM provider risks leaking that methodology, making prompt-level IP protection a major emerging concern for chip companies.
insights.speaker: Sathish Balasubramanian
insights.so_what: Chip design companies using cloud-hosted frontier LLMs for agentic design work may be inadvertently exposing proprietary design methodology; investors should watch for on-prem/air-gapped AI deployment becoming a purchasing requirement in semiconductor IP-sensitive segments.
insights.quote: Every prompt is necessary to the LLM providers. If it goes outside of the air gap, it’s a problem. So IP protection is going to be very key.
insights.locator: Balasubramanian: IP ownership is one of the biggest concerns

insights.claim: Under current U.S. copyright law, code/chip designs generated by AI are not copyrightable, and copyright requires that the majority of a design be human-authored -- a threshold Petr says is increasingly not being met as AI contribution to chip design grows.
insights.speaker: Alexander Petr
insights.so_what: A largely unaddressed legal exposure for the semiconductor industry: as AI's share of design work grows, more chips may fall outside copyright protection entirely, a risk factor for IP-dependent business models (e.g., IP licensing firms) that investors should track for regulatory/legal developments.
insights.quote: U.S. copyright does not allow us to copyright code that has been generated by an AI. That means every chip designed by an AI isn’t copyrightable... the majority is not going to be [done by a human].
insights.locator: Petr: Another problem is that U.S. copyright does not allow us

insights.claim: ChipAgents' proposed solution to both the IP-leakage and copyright problem is deploying a custom model fully on-premises: because the design never leaves the customer's environment, it functions as de facto proprietary IP even though it may not be formally copyrightable, though Petr cautions this doesn't eliminate reverse-engineering risk.
insights.speaker: Harrison Balistreri
insights.so_what: On-prem/custom-model deployment is emerging as the de facto industry response to both security and IP/copyright ambiguity in agentic chip design -- a product requirement investors should expect to see codified into enterprise AI-for-EDA contracts.
insights.quote: If the design never leaves your environment, it’s de facto still yours. It’s not copyrighted per se, but no one else can access it.
insights.locator: Balistreri: I want to recap a bit and then get to this point

themes.theme: Cost and security economics of agentic deployment

insights.claim: ChipAgents claims its harness-layer optimization lets the same underlying model perform like-for-like chip-design tasks using 40% fewer tokens than unoptimized deployment, and separately offers its own open-weight model performing similarly to frontier models at lower cost.
insights.speaker: Harrison Balistreri
insights.so_what: A concrete, vendor-stated efficiency benchmark (40% token reduction) for evaluating competing agentic EDA platforms on cost -- useful for modeling unit economics of AI-driven chip design tools.
insights.quote: The same model, doing like-for-like tasks, uses 40% fewer tokens.
insights.locator: Balistreri: There are many problems, many layers of problems

insights.claim: Balistreri frames sending chip-design inference over the public internet to frontier model providers as a direct competitive and security risk, because some of those same AI providers are themselves building chips that compete with the customer's chips, and not all frontier providers guarantee zero data retention.
insights.speaker: Harrison Balistreri
insights.so_what: A structural conflict-of-interest concern for semiconductor companies using AI labs that are simultaneously entering the chip market -- a factor likely to steer large chipmakers toward sovereign/on-prem models over frontier API providers.
insights.quote: Do you want to send your inference over the public internet to a model provider that is building chips that compete with your chips?
insights.locator: Balistreri: I want to recap a bit and then get to this point

themes.theme: Guardrails needed against infinite-loop / runaway token burn

insights.claim: IC design and verification are near-infinite problem spaces, so agentic AI deployments require pre-built infrastructure guardrails limiting how much time, how many tokens, and what scope a tool covers -- extending the same cost-control discipline EDA customers historically applied to CPU-cycle budgets to the new resource of AI tokens.
insights.speaker: Matt Graham
insights.so_what: EDA customers already run dedicated internal teams optimizing compute/cycle budgets; expect that same discipline and headcount to extend to managing agentic token budgets, a governance layer that agentic AI vendors will need to support natively.
insights.quote: There are still infinite problems in IC design and verification... there must be guardrails somewhere on how much time, how many tokens, and what the tool covers.
insights.locator: Graham: This is part of the prep before you deploy

insights.claim: Alexander Petr notes that infinite-loop problems are not new to mathematical/engineering optimization and that the EDA industry already has established solutions for managing them, implying the agentic-AI version of this problem is tractable rather than novel.
insights.speaker: Alexander Petr
insights.so_what: Tempers concern about agentic AI 'runaway' failure modes -- suggests existing EDA engineering discipline can be repurposed rather than requiring wholly new risk controls.
insights.quote: Infinite loops are not new to us. Every mathematical problem has infinite loops. If you get into those trenches, we have solutions.
insights.locator: Petr: Infinite loops are not new to us
